scenes.title: Editors & IDEs for Data Engineering
scenes.narration: The right editor multiplies your productivity, catching mistakes early and letting you navigate large codebases with ease.

scenes.title: Features That Matter
bullets: Syntax highlighting and linting flag errors before you even run the code.
An integrated debugger lets you step through logic instead of guessing.
Git integration shows changes and resolves conflicts without leaving the editor.
Remote and container support lets you edit code running on servers.
scenes.narration: A good editor highlights syntax and lints as you type, so many bugs surface before execution. A built-in debugger replaces guesswork with the ability to pause and inspect your program line by line. Native Git integration keeps diffs and conflict resolution close at hand, and remote support lets you work directly against code on a server or inside a container.

scenes.title: Editors vs. Notebooks
scenes.narration: An IDE like VS Code shines for writing production code, with strong version control, refactoring, and testing support. Notebooks like Jupyter excel at interactive exploration and showing charts inline, but they are notoriously hard to review and version. A common practice is to explore in a notebook, then move the mature logic into proper modules in an editor.

scenes.title: Setting Up Your Editor
scenes.narration: Configuring an editor for a project takes only a few steps. You add the Python extension, tell it which virtual environment interpreter to use, and turn on formatting when you save. Wiring up Git and any remote connections then completes a setup that stays consistent across the team.

scenes.text: Point your editor at the project's virtual environment — otherwise autocomplete and linting reference the wrong packages.
scenes.narration: The most impactful editor setting is selecting the correct interpreter. Aim it at your project's virtual environment so that completion, linting, and debugging all reflect the right dependencies.
